title: Travelers' Third-Quarter Profit Reaches $1.92 Billion With an 86.8% Combined Ratio as Catastrophe Losses Stay Moderate
summary: The US property and casualty insurer reported core earnings of $9.18 a share, record new business in its commercial unit and a $295 million asbestos reserve addition that trimmed otherwise favorable reserve development.
description:
Travelers Companies, one of the largest property and casualty insurers in the United States, reported strong third-quarter results on October 16, 2026, with profit slightly above last year's and an underwriting margin that remained wide. The numbers below come from two secondary reports, TradingView News and Grafa, which agree with each other on the main figures. The company's own release was not available for review, and one of the reports links to a regulatory filing dated October 16, so readers who need exact figures should consult Travelers' filing. The reports also differ in how much detail they give, and where only one source gives a number it is identified.

Start with profit. Travelers reported net income of $1.917 billion for the quarter, compared with $1.888 billion a year earlier. Diluted earnings per share were $9.04, up from $8.24. Core income, which strips out investment gains and losses and other items the company treats as non-recurring, was $1.947 billion, compared with $1.867 billion, and core earnings per share were $9.18, up from $8.14. Total revenues were $12.412 billion, according to TradingView, and net written premiums, the premiums for policies written in the period, were $11.48 billion. Net realized investment losses were $34 million before tax.

The key measure for an insurer is the combined ratio, which adds claims and expenses and divides by premiums. A figure below 100% means the insurer made an underwriting profit. Travelers' consolidated combined ratio was 86.8%, and its underlying combined ratio, which excludes catastrophe losses and changes to reserves for prior years, was 84.1%. Underwriting income before tax was $1.432 billion, and underlying underwriting income was $1.736 billion. The gap between the two ratios is explained by catastrophes and reserves. Catastrophe losses net of reinsurance were $538 million before tax, driven by severe wind and hail, according to TradingView. That is a meaningful amount, but it did not push the ratio above the mid-80s. Net favorable prior-year reserve development was $234 million. That figure includes a $295 million addition to asbestos reserves, so the favorable development in other lines was larger than the net number suggests. Asbestos claims relate to exposure decades ago and have been a recurring reserve issue for many US insurers.

Investment income helped. Net investment income was $1.098 billion before tax, or $908 million after tax, up 6% according to Grafa. Insurers earn income on the premiums they hold until claims are paid, and higher bond yields in recent years have raised that income.

The segment figures show where growth is coming from. Business Insurance, the largest unit, had net written premiums of $5.868 billion, up 3% from a year earlier. Retention, the share of customers who renewed, was 86%, and new business was a record $699 million, according to TradingView. Bond and Specialty, which sells surety and management liability coverage, wrote $1.209 billion, up 12%, led by surety, and the company noted improved renewal trends in management liability. Personal Insurance, which covers autos and homes for individuals, wrote $4.403 billion, down 7%, mainly because of the divested Canadian operations. TradingView says the unit's underlying combined ratio improved, but higher catastrophe activity weighed on results. The reports do not give a separate combined ratio for each segment.

On capital, Travelers returned $1.769 billion to shareholders in the quarter, including $1.508 billion of share repurchases. Book value per share was $141.48, and adjusted book value per share, which excludes unrealised investment effects, was $172.47. Neither report gives a return on equity or a chief executive comment, so this article does not characterise management's outlook.

What should readers take from the results? First, commercial insurance remains profitable. A record level of new business at a combined ratio in the mid-80s suggests that pricing is still adequate and that insurers are competing for customers without sacrificing margins. Second, weather remains a significant but manageable cost. Severe wind and hail drove the quarter's catastrophe losses, and a single large hurricane could change the picture in the fourth quarter. Third, legacy liabilities matter. The asbestos addition is a reminder that reserves reflect estimates of future payments, and those estimates can move.

For businesses buying insurance, strong insurer profits can affect negotiations. When underwriting margins are wide, brokers often argue for lower rate increases or broader terms, and competition for new business tends to rise. Insurers, for their part, point to higher claims costs from litigation and repair inflation as reasons to keep raising prices. The reports reviewed here do not describe Travelers' pricing trends in detail, so conclusions about rates should wait for the company's disclosures.

For homeowners and drivers, the personal lines result is more mixed. The unit's premiums fell because of the Canada sale, not because of falling US prices, and the catastrophe activity that weighed on the quarter is the type of event that tends to push up home insurance premiums over time. Our coverage of Ontario's auto insurance reform and German storm losses this week shows that weather and claims costs are being felt in several markets at once.

For investors, the results are best read as company-reported data. Earnings per share rising by roughly 10% to 13% from a year earlier while the combined ratio stays in the mid-80s is a strong outcome, but the share price response will depend on expectations that this article does not cover. Nothing here is a recommendation to buy or sell any security. Other insurers' results over the coming weeks will show whether Travelers' margins are typical or exceptional.
source_name: Travelers (as reported by TradingView and Grafa)
image_alt: Insurance documents and a pen on a desk (illustrative)
key_points: Travelers reported third-quarter 2026 net income of $1.917 billion, or $9.04 a diluted share, and core income of $1.947 billion, or $9.18 a share, up from $8.14 a year earlier.
The consolidated combined ratio was 86.8% and the underlying combined ratio, which excludes catastrophes and prior-year reserve changes, was 84.1%.
Catastrophe losses were $538 million before tax, driven by severe wind and hail, and net favorable prior-year reserve development was $234 million after a $295 million addition to asbestos reserves.

Net written premiums were $11.48 billion; Business Insurance grew 3% with a record $699 million of new business, Bond & Specialty grew 12% and Personal Insurance fell 7% because Canadian operations were divested.

The company returned $1.769 billion to shareholders, including $1.508 billion of buybacks, and book value per share was $141.48; figures come from two secondary reports and should be checked against the company filing.
why_it_matters: Travelers is one of the largest US commercial insurers, so its results show whether insurance pricing is still ahead of claims costs. A strong underwriting margin suggests that businesses and homeowners are still paying prices that cover losses, while the asbestos charge is a reminder that old liabilities can resurface.

title: UnitedHealth Raises 2026 Guidance as Its Medical Care Ratio Improves to 88.4%, but Membership Falls to 48.3 Million
summary: The largest US health insurer reported adjusted earnings of $4.69 a share and lifted its full-year outlook, helped by $610 million of favorable reserve development, while its insured membership and Optum Health revenue shrank.
description:
UnitedHealth Group, the largest health insurer in the United States, reported a sharp improvement in third-quarter profit on October 13, 2026 and raised its outlook for the year, even as the number of people it insures and the size of its care-delivery business both shrank. The figures come from the company's earnings release filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission and, for the management commentary, from an AI-assisted transcript of the earnings call published by The Motley Fool, which may contain errors and should be checked against the recording. The company's results matter well beyond its shareholders because it covers tens of millions of people and runs the pharmacy benefit and care businesses that sit under its Optum brand.

The headline numbers are these. Revenue was $112.7 billion, slightly below $113.2 billion a year earlier. Earnings from operations rose to $6.6 billion from $4.3 billion. Net earnings were $4.3 billion, up from $2.5 billion, with $4.1 billion attributable to shareholders. Diluted earnings per share were $4.56, compared with $2.59, and adjusted earnings per share were $4.69, compared with $2.92. The net margin was 3.6%, up from 2.1%. Operating cash flow was $5.1 billion, about 1.2 times net income. Year to date the company has repurchased $5.0 billion of shares and paid $6.2 billion in dividends. Its debt-to-capital ratio was 41.7%, against a target of about 40% by year-end.

The most important ratio for a health insurer is the medical care ratio, which shows how much of each premium dollar is paid out for medical care. UnitedHealth's was 88.4%, down from 89.9% a year earlier. That improvement includes $610 million of favorable prior-period reserve development, meaning the company's earlier estimates of medical costs proved higher than the amounts eventually paid. The operating cost ratio, which measures administrative costs against revenue, fell to 12.8% from 13.5%. Because favorable reserve development is a one-off benefit that lowers the current ratio, the underlying improvement is smaller than the headline change.

On guidance, the company raised its 2026 outlook. It now expects diluted earnings per share of at least $19.50 and adjusted earnings per share of at least $20.50. Management also said, according to the call transcript, that 2027 earnings should grow toward the lower end of its long-term target range of 13% to 16%, and that fuller 2027 guidance will come before the end of the year. It did not give membership guidance yet.

The segments show a mixed picture. UnitedHealthcare, the insurance arm, had revenue of $86.3 billion and operating earnings of $2.8 billion, a margin of 3.3%. It served 48.3 million people, down from 50.1 million a year earlier. Optum, the services arm, had revenue of $66.9 billion and operating earnings of $3.7 billion, a margin of 5.6%. Within Optum, Optum Health, which provides care and manages value-based care arrangements, had revenue of $22.9 billion, down 10% from a year earlier, with earnings of $735 million and a margin of 3.2%. The call transcript says the drop reflects fewer value-based care patients in some markets and that management targets a margin of 6% to 8% over time on a gradual path. Optum Insight, which sells data and technology services, had revenue of $5.5 billion, up 3%, with a margin of 23.4%. Optum Rx, the pharmacy benefit manager, had revenue of $39.9 billion and a margin of 4.3%, and adjusted prescriptions fell to 393 million from 414 million, mainly because of the loss of UnitedHealthcare members, according to the transcript.

What did management say about costs? According to the transcript, the commercial benefit cost trend is above 11%, driven by arbitration awards under the No Surprises Act, greater intensity of care from clinicians and high-cost specialty drugs. Management described the trend as stabilising but still elevated, and said it argues that arbitration awards are excessive and contribute to a lack of affordability while supporting the intent of the law. It also said costs for specialty pharmacy and high-intensity hospital care remain stubbornly high. In Medicare Advantage, it expects its margin near the top of a 2% to 4% range and said about 75% of members are expected to be in plans rated four stars or higher for payment year 2028, compared with a 70% industry average. For Medicaid, the company expects results moderately better than negative 1% in 2026, which it called a trough year, while noting that state funding has not kept pace with cost trends.

Management also pointed to artificial intelligence. The transcript says AI chart summarisation reaches more than 40% of employed clinicians and cuts chart review time by 33%, that appeal cycle times are 26% shorter, and that prior authorisations are expected to fall 30% by the end of 2026. These are company statements that have not been independently verified.

What does this mean for the public? Three points stand out. First, health costs are still rising faster than many employers and individuals would like, and a commercial trend above 11% is likely to feed into premiums for 2027. Second, the shrinking membership suggests the company is pruning where it competes, which can affect the choices available to seniors during Medicare open enrollment, which began on October 15. Third, the improvement in profit came with a smaller revenue base, so it does not show that care has become cheaper.

For investors, the numbers show a company recovering margins after a difficult period, with guidance raised, but with open questions about growth, because membership and Optum Health revenue are falling. This article describes company-reported results and is not a recommendation to buy or sell any security. The company's 2027 guidance, due before year-end, and the premium filings of health plans in the coming weeks will show how much of the recent cost pressure is being passed on to customers.
source_name: UnitedHealth Group (SEC filing and earnings call transcript)
key_points: UnitedHealth reported third-quarter 2026 revenue of $112.7 billion, net earnings of $4.3 billion, diluted EPS of $4.56 and adjusted EPS of $4.69, compared with $2.92 a year earlier.
The medical care ratio improved to 88.4% from 89.9%, including $610 million of favorable prior-period reserve development, and the operating cost ratio fell to 12.8%.
The company raised 2026 guidance to at least $19.50 in diluted EPS and at least $20.50 in adjusted EPS.
UnitedHealthcare served 48.3 million people, down from 50.1 million a year earlier; Optum Health revenue fell 10% to $22.9 billion and Optum Rx adjusted scripts fell to 393 million.
Management said commercial cost trend is above 11% and stabilising, expects Medicare Advantage margin near the top of 2% to 4%, and expects 2027 earnings growth toward the low end of 13% to 16%.
why_it_matters: UnitedHealth is the biggest private player in American health coverage, so its costs and membership show what is happening to health spending. Rising medical costs, shrinking enrolment and tighter margins affect the premiums employers pay, the plans seniors can choose and how health insurers decide where to compete.

title: UK Economy Grows 0.1% in August, Beating Forecasts of a Fall, as Services Stall Ahead of the October 28 Budget
summary: The ONS says GDP rose 0.7% in the three months to August, the eighth consecutive rise, but services were flat in the month, construction fell again and analysts warn higher energy prices could lift inflation.
description:
The United Kingdom's economy grew a little in August, beating expectations of a decline, but the detail behind the headline shows an economy that is being carried by a narrow set of sectors while households hold back. The Office for National Statistics published its monthly GDP estimate on October 15, 2026. The release comes two weeks before the government's Budget, at a time when energy prices are rising and interest rates are higher than many borrowers would like, which makes every data point more closely watched than usual.

Start with the numbers from the ONS bulletin. GDP rose by 0.1% in August. That follows growth of 0.4% in July, which the ONS left unrevised, and 0.4% in June, which was revised up from 0.3%. Over the three months to August, GDP rose 0.7% compared with the three months to May, the eighth consecutive three-month rise, and the two preceding three-month periods were each revised up to 0.5%. GDP in the latest three months is 1.8% higher than in the same three months a year earlier, and August itself is 2.1% higher than August 2025. Euronews reports that economists had expected a contraction of 0.1% for the month, so the outturn was better than forecast, although it marked a slowdown from July.

The sector breakdown is where the story is more nuanced. Over the three months, services grew 0.9% and were the only broad sector to rise, which made them the main driver of growth. Production fell 0.2%, after a revised fall of 0.7% in the three months to July. Construction fell 1.0%, with both new work and repair and maintenance declining. In August alone, production rose 0.8%, led by manufacturing, while services were flat and construction fell 0.2%, its fourth consecutive monthly decline. The ONS also noted that the first estimate of July construction was revised down to a fall of 0.5%, from growth of 0.1%, after new returns from several firms replaced estimated figures. ONS director of economic statistics Liz McKeown said computer programming was once again the largest contributor to growth in the three months to August, according to Euronews, which also reports that growth in the artificial intelligence sector helped drive the expansion in July.

The Euronews headline refers to a fall in consumer spending, although the article does not give figures for household spending or consumer-facing services, and the ONS summary reviewed here does not either. That limits what can be said about shops, restaurants and leisure businesses. What the reports do indicate is a split between businesses and households. Paul Dales of Capital Economics said the coming rise in inflation should still dampen growth, but that the economy is more robust than he thought. He described a division in which businesses are performing well, partly because of AI-related spending, while households are becoming more cautious.

Inflation and interest rates are the backdrop. An economic overview published on October 6 reported that consumer price inflation was 3.1% in the twelve months to August, up from 2.9% in July, with core inflation at 2.6%. It also reported that the Bank of England held its rate at 3.75% on September 17, with three of nine members voting for a rise to 4%. Unemployment was 4.9% in the three months to July and wage growth excluding bonuses was 3.5%. Euronews adds that analysts expect inflation to rise toward the end of the year as higher oil and gas prices pass through to household bills, with no sign of the conflict in the Middle East ending soon, and that Samuel Edwards of Ebury warned that energy prices could reignite inflation and might push the Bank of England to raise rates further. These are analyst views, not official forecasts.

The Budget is the other event to watch. Euronews says it will be presented on October 28 and that the government has pledged to maintain strict fiscal discipline without saying whether new tax rises will be included. It also reports that government bond yields have reached multi-decade highs. Edwards warned that further tax rises could lead consumers to cut spending and businesses to hold back investment, and noted that the International Monetary Fund's gloomier outlook for 2027 suggests the UK is not out of trouble.

What does it mean for people and businesses? For households with variable-rate mortgages or loans, the risk is that inflation pushes the Bank of England to raise rates again, which would raise repayments. For people on fixed rates, the main issue is what happens when they next refinance. For savers, higher rates help deposits, though inflation reduces the real value of savings. For insurance buyers, rising inflation lifts the cost of repairs and replacement, which feeds into premiums, so sums insured should be reviewed to avoid underinsurance. For businesses, the AI-linked strength in technology services is a bright spot, but weakness in construction and production over the quarter shows that gains are not spread evenly.

There are also limits to what one month of data can show. Monthly GDP figures are volatile and are revised, as the August release itself shows with the changes to June and July construction. The ONS cautions that its estimates incorporate revisions in line with the quarterly national accounts and Blue Book 2026, which means earlier numbers can change. A single month of 0.1% growth is not a trend.

The next steps are clear. The Budget on October 28 and the next GDP release on November 12 will show whether the economy can keep growing as energy costs rise and fiscal policy tightens. Readers should treat the forecasts quoted here as opinions and look to the ONS and the Bank of England for official figures.
image_alt: Office towers in a business district (illustrative)
key_points: UK GDP rose 0.1% in August 2026 after growth of about 0.4% in July and 0.4% in June (revised up from 0.3%), and rose 0.7% in the three months to August, the eighth consecutive three-month rise.
Economists had expected a small fall; production rose 0.8% in August, led by manufacturing, while services were flat and construction fell 0.2%, its fourth consecutive monthly fall.
Over the three months, services rose 0.9%, production fell 0.2% and construction fell 1.0%; GDP is 2.1% higher than in August 2025.

Euronews reports analysts expect inflation to rise toward year-end as energy prices pass through, and that the Budget is due on October 28; the Bank of England held its rate at 3.75% in September with three members voting to raise it.
The ONS says computer programming was the largest contributor to growth in the three months to August; the next GDP release is due on November 12.
why_it_matters: Growth that is stronger than forecast eases fears of a downturn, but the details show an economy leaning on a few sectors while households grow cautious. Together with rising energy costs and an imminent Budget, that shapes borrowing costs, insurance premiums and the prices people pay.

title: HDFC Life's Half-Year Profit Rises 13% to Rs 1,119 Crore as New Business Value Grows 12%, While Proposed Expense Rules Loom
summary: India's HDFC Life reported first-half value of new business of Rs 2,037 crore at a 24.7% margin, approved a GIFT City office and up to Rs 500 crore of subordinated debt, and flagged near-term friction from IRDAI's proposed expense limits.
description:
HDFC Life Insurance reported higher profit and new business value for the six months ended September 30, 2026, while telling investors it expects some disruption from proposed changes to the way Indian regulators limit insurers' costs. The company's board approved the results on October 15, 2026. This article draws on three secondary reports of the company's disclosures, from ScanX, Kalkine and Whalesbook. Only the half-year figures are given in detail, and the reports do not provide separate standalone figures for the second quarter, so this article does not either. Readers who want exact numbers should consult the filing on the stock exchanges.

The headline numbers, according to ScanX, are these. Profit after tax for the half-year was Rs 1,119 crore, up about 13% from Rs 994 crore a year earlier. Value of new business, or VNB, which estimates the present value of profits from policies sold in the period, was Rs 2,037 crore, up about 12% from Rs 1,818 crore. The VNB margin, which is VNB divided by annualised premium equivalent, was 24.7%, compared with 24.5%. Annualised premium equivalent, a measure of new business sales that puts single and regular premiums on a common annual basis, was Rs 8,245 crore, up 11% from Rs 7,413 crore, and individual annualised premium equivalent was Rs 7,080 crore, up 9%. Total premium income was Rs 39,569 crore, up 16%. Assets under management were Rs 4,09,673 crore, up 14% from Rs 3,59,999 crore, and Indian embedded value, a measure of the value of the existing business plus net assets, was Rs 66,461 crore, up 12%.

A few of the quality indicators moved the wrong way. The total expense ratio rose to 22.3% from 21.6%. The 13-month persistency ratio, which shows the share of policies still in force after a year, fell to 83% from 86%. The 61-month persistency ratio improved to 66% from 62%, which suggests that longer-term policyholders are staying. The solvency ratio, a regulatory measure of capital strength, rose to 180% from 175%. Renewal collections grew 14%. In protection, retail protection grew 33% and made up about 8% of individual annualised premium equivalent, compared with about 7% a year earlier. ScanX also reports that individual weighted received premium grew 11% in the second quarter, compared with a private-industry average of 10%, and that the company's market share rose to 16.2% from 16.1% in the first quarter.

The board also approved two corporate actions, according to Kalkine. It gave in-principle approval for the issue of subordinated non-convertible debentures of up to Rs 500 crore, in one or more tranches on a private placement basis, with the final size, coupon and timing not yet disclosed. Subordinated debt counts toward an insurer's regulatory capital and ranks below policyholders and other creditors. The board also approved setting up an insurance office in the GIFT City international financial services centre in Gujarat, which needs approval from the Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India, the IFSC Authority and shareholders through a postal ballot. No dividend recommendation was made at the meeting.

The more significant story is the regulatory backdrop. According to Whalesbook, the Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India has proposed stricter limits on management expenses and distributor commissions, with the central item being the expense of management limits that cap how much insurers can spend on distribution, advertising and administration. The report does not give the proposed cap levels or a date for final notification. Our earlier coverage of the proposals in this series described them as caps on commissions that regulators are still weighing, and they should be treated as proposals until the regulator issues final rules. HDFC Life's management, as paraphrased by Whalesbook, said it expects a period of operational adjustment and is prepared to adapt. It cited an expense ratio of roughly 21% for the recent quarter, a figure that is not directly comparable with the 22.3% half-year ratio reported by ScanX because the periods differ. Management said it prefers to manage adjustments through market dynamics rather than fixed numerical targets, pointed to the 2017 changes to commission structures as a precedent in which the industry kept growing, especially through banks, and said it relies on its product mix, including a growing annuity portfolio and a stable bancassurance network, to absorb volatility. It also expects the upcoming risk-based capital framework to ease solvency constraints. These are paraphrases of remarks by management, not direct quotes.

What does this mean for policyholders? If final rules cut the amount insurers can spend on distribution, the effect could appear in several places. Commissions paid to agents and banks could fall, which might change who sells which products and how hard they are pushed. Insurers might redesign products to keep margins, or pass some savings to customers, though the reports reviewed do not say which is more likely. For customers, the useful advice does not change. Compare premiums and benefits across insurers, check the claim settlement record, and avoid buying a product simply because it earns a high commission for the seller. The fall in 13-month persistency at HDFC Life is a reminder to buy only what you can afford to keep paying, since early lapses often mean lost money.

What should investors watch? The key variables are the final form and timing of the expense rules, the trend in the VNB margin as costs and mix change, and persistency, which affects long-term profit. The reports include some views on risks, such as margin pressure if rules require significant spending cuts and the possibility that distributors need time to adjust to new payout models, which could reduce volumes. This article describes company-reported results and is not investment advice.

HDFC Life's results arrive two days after ICICI Life's, which we covered separately. Together they suggest that the largest private life insurers are growing profits at a double-digit pace, with protection products growing faster than the rest, while preparing for a tougher cost environment. The regulator's final decision on expense limits will decide how comfortable that outlook turns out to be.
source_name: ScanX, Kalkine and Whalesbook (reporting HDFC Life disclosures)
image_alt: Financial statements and a calculator on a desk (illustrative)
key_points: HDFC Life's board approved results on October 15, 2026: first-half profit after tax of Rs 1,119 crore, up about 13%, and value of new business of Rs 2,037 crore, up about 12%, with a margin of 24.7%.
Total annualised premium equivalent was Rs 8,245 crore, up 11%; total premium income was Rs 39,569 crore, up 16%; assets under management were Rs 4.10 lakh crore, up 14%.
The total expense ratio rose to 22.3% from 21.6%, 13-month persistency fell to 83% from 86%, and the solvency ratio was 180%.

The board gave in-principle approval to up to Rs 500 crore of subordinated debentures and to an insurance office at GIFT City, subject to IRDAI, IFSC Authority and shareholder approvals; no dividend was recommended.
Management told analysts it expects near-term friction from IRDAI's proposed expense and commission limits, which are still proposals, and cited the industry's 2017 adjustment as a precedent.
why_it_matters: India's private life insurers are about to face tighter limits on how much they can spend on distribution. HDFC Life's numbers show a profitable business with a falling persistency rate and rising expenses, which is the setting in which rule changes could affect commissions, products and prices for customers.

title: Canada Loses 68,000 Jobs in September and Unemployment Rises to 6.5%, Complicating the Bank of Canada's October 28 Decision
summary: Public-sector and education job losses, a sharp fall for young workers and the lowest participation rate in 29 years outside the pandemic left markets cutting bets on a rate rise, even as inflation runs near 3%.
description:
Canada's labour market weakened sharply in September, giving the Bank of Canada a harder decision at its October 28 meeting. Statistics Canada's Labour Force Survey, released on October 9, 2026, showed the economy shed about 68,000 jobs, after a loss of about 42,000 in August, and the unemployment rate rose to 6.5% from 6.4%. The figures are described here as reported by Advisor.ca and Babypips, which differ slightly in places, for example on the exact August loss, and where they differ the article says so. The next jobs report is due on November 6.

Start with the size of the surprise. Economists polled before the release expected the economy to add about 9,000 jobs, according to both reports, so the actual result was roughly 77,000 below the forecast. Advisor.ca describes it as the steepest monthly job loss since February. The losses were split nearly evenly between full-time and part-time work, with Babypips reporting a fall of 35,400 full-time and 32,900 part-time jobs. The unemployment rate rose by 0.1 percentage points to 6.5%, back to its level in January, which is in line with forecasts. Babypips notes that the rate was held down because fewer people were searching for work, as the participation rate fell to 64.8% from 65.0%, the lowest reading in 29 years outside the pandemic period. The article points to an ageing population and slower immigration as reasons.

Where were the jobs lost? According to Advisor.ca, the losses were concentrated in the public sector, which has now declined for four straight months, while the private sector was stable, which economists found reassuring. Educational services led the industry losses with about 35,000 fewer jobs, followed by health care and manufacturing. Babypips reports that education, health care and social assistance together lost 58,400 jobs and manufacturing lost 12,700, and that Statistics Canada linked part of the fall in education to fewer international students. Young workers were hard hit: those aged 15 to 24 lost 48,000 jobs, and women aged 25 to 54 also saw employment fall. Repair, maintenance and household and personal services gained 17,000.

The provincial picture varied. Quebec lost 49,000 jobs, Ontario 20,000 and British Columbia 20,000, while Alberta added 23,000, according to Advisor.ca. Wages rose, with Babypips reporting that average hourly pay for permanent employees was up 2.3% from a year earlier, compared with 2.0% in August. That is below the rate of inflation, which means real wages are falling. On a longer view, Babypips says Canada has lost a net 41,200 jobs so far in 2026, compared with a gain of 211,300 over the same period last year, while Advisor.ca says employment is up 95,000 from a year ago and that employers added 181,000 jobs from April to July. These two statements are not necessarily inconsistent, since they cover different periods, but they show how the monthly weakness follows a stronger spring and summer.

Economists' reactions were pointed but not uniform. Robert Kavcic of BMO called it a very bad jobs print but noted that smoothed six-month trends still show modest, steady gains. Daniel Hyun of KPMG said it would be premature to blame tariffs, since most losses came from sectors that do not face trade directly. Andrew Hencic of TD said he expects the Bank of Canada to hold this month, with two weak labour reports undermining arguments for a rate rise. Babypips adds that economists see the effect of United States tariffs on employment data as limited.

The central bank's dilemma is the key point. The Bank of Canada held its overnight rate at 2.25% on September 2, and the next decision is scheduled for Wednesday, October 28 at 9:45 a.m. Eastern. Its September statement said consumer price inflation had been about 3% in recent months, mainly because of gasoline prices, and that upside risks to inflation had increased because of the conflict in the Middle East and tariffs. August inflation was 3.0%, according to Babypips, well above the 2% target. Against that, weak hiring argues for patience. According to Advisor.ca, LSEG data put the probability of a quarter-point hike in October at about 25%, down from about 40% before the jobs data. KPMG still expects a rise to 2.5% by year-end, but Hyun said the soft data adds doubt to a December move, while Babypips says traders now price a possible 25 basis point hike in December. September inflation data, due on October 19 according to Babypips, will be the next important input.

The currency also reacted. Advisor.ca reports the Canadian dollar fell to its lowest level against the US dollar since early 2025, briefly dipping below 70 US cents, and Babypips reports a fall of 0.44% to 1.4287 per US dollar and a drop of 9.5 basis points in the two-year yield to 2.410% after the release. A weaker currency makes imports more expensive, which can add to inflation, a further complication for policymakers.

What does it mean for households? For mortgage holders, the immediate effect is uncertainty. Renewing borrowers face a rate environment in which a hike is possible but less likely than before the data, and our earlier coverage of mortgage renewals notes that many borrowers are already renewing at higher payments. For workers, especially young people and those in education and public services, the data signal tougher hiring. For savers, any rate rise would lift deposit rates, while a hold keeps them where they are. For lenders and insurers, rising unemployment is an early indicator of credit stress and can lead to more missed payments, although the data do not yet show that.

Readers should keep two cautions in mind. Monthly survey estimates are volatile and subject to sampling error, and economists such as BMO's note the underlying trend is better than one month. And the sources here are secondary reports of the Statistics Canada release, so exact figures should be confirmed on the agency's website. The coming CPI release and the October 28 decision will show which concern wins out.
source_name: Statistics Canada (as reported by Advisor.ca and Babypips)
key_points: Canada lost about 68,000 jobs in September after about 42,000 in August; economists had expected a gain of about 9,000, and the unemployment rate rose to 6.5% from 6.4%.
Losses were concentrated in the public sector, which has fallen four straight months; educational services lost about 35,000, workers aged 15 to 24 lost 48,000, and the private sector was stable.
By province, Quebec lost 49,000 jobs, Ontario 20,000 and British Columbia 20,000, while Alberta added 23,000.
Babypips reports the participation rate fell to 64.8%, the lowest in 29 years outside the pandemic era, and average hourly wages for permanent employees rose 2.3% from a year earlier.

The Bank of Canada's rate is 2.25% with inflation near 3%; LSEG data cited by Advisor.ca put the chance of an October rate rise at about 25%, down from about 40% before the data, with the next decision on October 28.
why_it_matters: The Bank of Canada must balance inflation near 3% against a weakening labour market. Whether it raises, holds or waits will affect mortgage renewals, loan costs and savings returns for millions of households, and weak hiring can also change how insurers and lenders see credit risk.

title: Germany Raises Its 2026 Growth Forecast to 1.3% From 0.5%, but the Economy Minister Says the Recovery Stands on 'Shaky Legs'
summary: The government's autumn projection credits exports and state spending, while inflation hit 3.3% in September and employment is falling, leaving business groups warning that debt-financed support has a short shelf life.
description:
Germany's government has sharply raised its growth forecast for 2026, but the same week brought evidence that the recovery is narrower and shakier than the headline implies. The Federal Government published its autumn economic projection on Thursday, October 8, 2026, with Economy Minister Katherina Reiche presenting the figures, according to reports by the German outlets cash-online.de and ZDFheute. Five days later, the federal statistics office reported that inflation had climbed to its highest level in almost three years. Reading the two together gives a more balanced picture. This article translates and summarises those German-language reports for an international audience.

The headline forecast is an upgrade. The government now expects real GDP to grow 1.3% in 2026, up from 0.5% in its spring projection of April 22, a rise of 0.8 percentage points. It expects growth of 1.1% in 2027, up from 0.9%, and 0.6% in 2028, for which the spring projection gave no figure. A joint forecast by five economic institutes, DIW Berlin, ifo, the Kiel Institute, IWH Halle and RWI Essen, published on September 24, matches the government's numbers for 2026 and 2027 and expects 0.4% for 2028. The BDI, the industry federation, has also raised its 2026 forecast, from 0.6% to 1.0%, according to cash-online.

What explains the upgrade? The economy ministry said that the economy was robust in the first half of 2026 despite the conflict in the Middle East and higher energy prices, with the main impulses coming from exports and high government spending. In the second quarter, exporters benefited from what the ministry called a special development: because of global bottlenecks, energy-intensive goods made in Germany were put into storage, which boosted measured output. The government's special fund for defence and infrastructure is also contributing. The reports describe a 500 billion euro special fund for infrastructure and climate neutrality spread over twelve years, comprising 300 billion for federal investment, 100 billion for states and municipalities and 100 billion for the Climate and Transformation Fund. Second-quarter GDP rose 0.3% on the quarter, first reported as 0.2%, and 1.0% on the year. Goods exports rose 2.6% in that period, but exports fell 0.8% in August.

The weak spots are significant. Equipment investment fell 1.4%, and private consumption and investment remain weak. Employment in the second quarter was 0.5% lower than a year earlier, a drop of about 212,000 people, even though the economy grew. According to Destatis, employment in services is shrinking for the first time since the pandemic. That combination, output rising while jobs fall, is unusual and suggests that the growth is being driven by sectors and measures that do not create much work.

Inflation adds to the pressure. The statistics office Destatis reported on October 13 that consumer prices rose 3.3% in September from a year earlier, up from 2.9% in August and 2.8% in July, the highest rate since December 2023. Prices rose 0.6% from August. Energy prices were up 14.9% on the year, driven by motor fuels, up 37.1%, and heating oil, up 74.9%, while electricity, natural gas and district heating became cheaper. Core inflation, excluding food and energy, was 2.4%, below the overall rate. Food prices rose 0.4%, goods prices 3.8% and services prices 2.7%, slightly slower. A federal fuel tax cut took effect on October 1, so it is not reflected in the September figures. The government's spring projection had assumed inflation of 2.7% for 2026 and 2.8% for 2027, and the reports reviewed did not give the autumn inflation forecast, so it is not clear how it compares.

The people who presented and commented on the forecast were cautious. Reiche, speaking the day before publication, described the situation as fragile and growth as being on shaky legs, according to ZDFheute. She called for structural reforms, including more flexible working hours, stable social contributions, less bureaucracy and competitive energy prices. The DIHK, the chambers of commerce association, warned that debt-financed state spending has only a short shelf life and saw no independent export momentum, citing trade policy uncertainty and location disadvantages. The BGA, the foreign trade association, described firms as operating with the handbrake on. BDI chief executive Tanja Gönner, by contrast, said the outlook for Germany is improving. The coverage notes that experts consider the growth insufficient in the long term and that labour market measures and the planned pension reform are politically contested in the governing coalition.

Risks cut both ways. The ministry said further developments depend on the conflicts in the Middle East and Ukraine, and that a lasting resolution could lower energy prices and speed the recovery. Persistently high prices continue to burden companies and households. The closing advice in the cash-online article is to treat the upturn as temporary, because it rests on exports and state investment rather than private demand.

What does it mean for households and businesses? For workers, the fall in employment in services is a warning even as the headline numbers improve. For households, inflation of 3.3% erodes purchasing power, and heating oil and fuel are the main culprits, although the fuel tax cut from October 1 should ease pump prices. For insurers and lenders, inflation raises repair and replacement costs and can increase claims, while weak private investment limits demand for business loans. For savers and borrowers across the euro area, the European Central Bank's next meeting will weigh German inflation heavily, though this article does not forecast its decision.

The fair reading is that the forecast upgrade is real but fragile. A government-backed investment programme and stockpiling are lifting measured growth, while jobs, equipment investment and private consumption lag. The next tests are the October inflation figure, which will show the effect of the fuel tax cut, and whether exports recover after August's fall. Readers should treat all forecasts here as projections, not certainties, and consult the Federal Government's published projection for exact figures.
source_name: German Federal Government and Destatis (via cash-online.de and ZDFheute)
image_alt: Data lines over a globe representing economic forecasts (illustrative)
key_points: The German government's autumn projection of October 8 raises 2026 growth to 1.3% from 0.5% in April, with 1.1% for 2027 (up from 0.9%) and 0.6% for 2028.
A joint forecast by five research institutes published on September 24 matches the government on 2026 and 2027 and expects 0.4% for 2028.

Second-quarter GDP rose 0.3% on the quarter and 1.0% on the year, helped by exports and by stockpiling of energy-intensive goods, but employment fell 0.5% from a year earlier and goods exports fell 0.8% in August.

Destatis reported on October 13 that inflation rose to 3.3% in September, the highest since December 2023, with energy up 14.9% and core inflation at 2.4%; a federal fuel tax cut took effect on October 1.
Economy Minister Katherina Reiche called growth fragile and urged reforms; the DIHK warned that debt-financed state spending has a short shelf life.
why_it_matters: Germany is Europe's largest economy, so its outlook affects exports, jobs and borrowing costs across the continent. Higher growth forecasts are welcome, but a recovery that depends on exports and state spending while prices and unemployment rise is less secure than the headline suggests.
